text: Which Azure AI capability extracts fields such as totals and dates from scanned invoices and receipts?
options: A) Azure AI Document Intelligence
B) Azure AI Translator
C) Azure AI Speech
D) Azure AI Content Safety
correctAnswerText: A) Azure AI Document Intelligence
explanation: Azure AI Document Intelligence, formerly Form Recognizer, extracts structured fields from documents rather than returning raw text. Prebuilt models understand common document types such as invoices, receipts, identity documents, and tax forms, returning typed fields like totals, dates, and line items along with confidence scores. Custom models can be trained on a small number of examples for forms specific to an organization. This is what distinguishes it from plain optical character recognition, which returns text without knowing what any of it means.
whyOthersWrong: The others translate text, work with speech, or screen content for harmful material.

whyWrong.B: Translator converts text between languages.
whyWrong.C: Speech handles transcription and synthesis.
whyWrong.D: Content Safety detects harmful content.

text: What does automated machine learning provide?
options: A) It labels the training data automatically
B) It guarantees that the resulting model is free of bias
C) It tries many algorithms and settings automatically and ranks the resulting models
D) It deploys models without any compute resources
correctAnswerText: C) It tries many algorithms and settings automatically and ranks the resulting models
explanation: Automated machine learning takes a prepared dataset, a target column, and a metric to optimize, then trains many candidate models across different algorithms and preprocessing choices and presents them ranked by that metric. It compresses the slow part of early experimentation and gives a defensible baseline that a hand-built model has to beat to justify its cost. What it does not do is supply the data: labelling, cleaning, and deciding whether the features are appropriate remain human work, and so does judging fairness, which requires examining outcomes across groups rather than reading a single score. Training still consumes compute, which is provisioned and billed as usual.
whyOthersWrong: The others label data, promise fairness, or remove the need for compute, none of which automation supplies.

whyWrong.A: Labelling is a separate task; automated training needs labelled data as input.
whyWrong.B: Fairness must be assessed deliberately and is not guaranteed by any training run.
whyWrong.D: Training and deployment both consume compute that is billed.

text: What is a device twin in Azure IoT Hub?
options: A) A second physical device kept as a spare
B) A duplicate of the hub in a paired region
C) A simulator used to test the solution before hardware arrives
D) A JSON document in the cloud holding the device's reported state and its desired configuration
correctAnswerText: D) A JSON document in the cloud holding the device's reported state and its desired configuration
explanation: Each device registered with IoT Hub has a twin: a JSON document stored in the service containing tags, properties the device reports about itself, and properties the solution desires it to have. A back-end application sets a desired property and the device applies it whenever it is next connected, which is how configuration reaches fleets that are intermittently offline without anyone holding a live session. Reported properties travel the other way, so the hub always holds the last known state even while the device is asleep. Twins can also be queried in bulk, which is how a fleet is filtered by firmware version or by any tag the solution assigns.
whyOthersWrong: The others describe spare hardware, a regional copy of the service, or a simulator, while a twin is a state document for one device.

whyWrong.A: A twin is data in the cloud, not a second piece of hardware.
whyWrong.B: It represents one device, not a copy of the hub.
whyWrong.C: Simulated devices are a testing technique, unrelated to twins.

text: A retailer needs to run analytics and machine learning on a factory floor with intermittent connectivity, sending only summarized results to the cloud. Which approach fits?
options: A) Send all raw telemetry to Azure Stream Analytics in the cloud
B) Deploy Azure IoT Edge modules on a local gateway device
C) Use Azure Data Box to ship data weekly
D) Install Azure Arc on each sensor
correctAnswerText: B) Deploy Azure IoT Edge modules on a local gateway device
explanation: Azure IoT Edge moves cloud workloads down to a local gateway device, running them as containerized modules that can include Stream Analytics jobs, machine learning models, Azure Functions, and custom code. Because processing happens locally, the site keeps operating during connectivity loss and only summarized results are sent upstream, which also reduces bandwidth cost. Modules are deployed and updated from IoT Hub, so the fleet is managed centrally even though the compute is distributed. Offline buffering means messages produced during an outage are forwarded once the link returns.
whyOthersWrong: The others depend on the connection that is unreliable, batch the data far too slowly, or apply to servers rather than sensors.

whyWrong.A: Sending all raw telemetry to the cloud requires the connectivity the site does not have.
whyWrong.C: Shipping data weekly cannot support real-time factory decisions.
whyWrong.D: Azure Arc manages servers and clusters, not individual sensors.

text: What distinguishes an event from a message in an Azure messaging architecture?
options: A) An event is encrypted while a message is sent in clear text
B) Events are delivered in order while messages are not
C) An event is a lightweight notification that something happened; a message carries data the receiver is expected to process
D) An event can only be sent between resources in the same region
correctAnswerText: C) An event is a lightweight notification that something happened; a message carries data the receiver is expected to process
explanation: An event announces a fact — a blob was created, a resource was deleted — and the publisher neither knows nor cares what any subscriber does about it, so the payload is typically small and may carry only a reference to the thing that changed. A message is sent with an expectation: the sender has a contract with the receiver, the content is the work item itself, and delivery guarantees matter. That distinction is what separates Event Grid and Event Hubs from Service Bus, and choosing the wrong side leads either to a broker used for simple notifications or to an event service asked for guarantees it does not offer. Ordering, encryption, and regional reach are configuration details rather than the difference between the two.
whyOthersWrong: The others draw the line at encryption, ordering, or region, while the real distinction is whether the publisher expects specific processing.

whyWrong.A: Both are protected in transit; encryption does not define the difference.
whyWrong.B: Ordering is a property of the chosen service, not of events as a category.
whyWrong.D: Events can be delivered across regions and to external endpoints.

text: A workload must deliver a large software update to users in 40 countries with low latency and reduced load on the origin server. Which combination is the most appropriate?
options: A) Store the files in Azure Blob Storage and serve them through a content delivery network
B) Store the files on a single virtual machine with a public IP address
C) Replicate the files to a storage account in each country manually
D) Serve the files from Azure Files over SMB
correctAnswerText: A) Store the files in Azure Blob Storage and serve them through a content delivery network
explanation: Storing the files once in Blob Storage and serving them through a content delivery network puts cached copies at edge locations close to users in every country, which is what removes both the latency of a long round trip and the load on the origin. Cache behaviour is controlled by expiry headers and rules, and content can be purged when a new version is published. Egress is billed at CDN rates from the edge rather than repeatedly from the origin region. Azure Front Door provides the same caching alongside global routing and a web application firewall.
whyOthersWrong: The others centralize on one server, create manual copies to maintain, or use a protocol unsuited to internet distribution.

whyWrong.B: A single virtual machine is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
whyWrong.C: Manual per-country copies are costly to maintain and still lack edge caching.
whyWrong.D: SMB file shares are not intended for public internet distribution.

text: An architect must design a solution that keeps a web tier running during the loss of one datacenter within a region, restores service in a second region after a regional outage, and keeps management ports closed by default. Which combination of Azure capabilities meets all three requirements?
options: A) Virtual machines in a single availability set, geo-redundant storage, and a network security group allowing RDP from the internet
B) A single large virtual machine with premium disks, Azure Backup, and a public IP address
C) Virtual machines in one zone, zone-redundant storage, and Azure Firewall in the same subnet
D) Virtual machines spread across availability zones, Azure Site Recovery replication to a paired region, and just-in-time access with Azure Bastion
correctAnswerText: D) Virtual machines spread across availability zones, Azure Site Recovery replication to a paired region, and just-in-time access with Azure Bastion
explanation: The three requirements map to three distinct capabilities. Spreading the web tier across availability zones keeps it running when one datacenter within the region is lost, since zones have independent power, cooling, and networking. Azure Site Recovery replicates the workload to the paired region and orchestrates failover, which covers the loss of the entire region with a defined recovery time and recovery point. Just-in-time access with Azure Bastion keeps management ports closed by default and removes the need for public IP addresses on the machines. Recognizing that each requirement needs its own control, rather than one service covering all three, is the point of the question.
whyOthersWrong: The others leave a single point of failure, expose management ports to the internet, or lack any cross-region recovery.

whyWrong.A: An availability set does not survive the loss of a building, and open RDP from the internet violates the third requirement.
whyWrong.B: One virtual machine with a public IP fails all three requirements.
whyWrong.C: A single zone gives no protection against losing that datacenter, and there is no cross-region recovery.
